questions.q_en:

I had heard of henpecked husbands and now, I felt that I saw one.
questions.q_hi:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.

I had heard of henpecked husbands and now, I felt that I saw one.
questions.solution_en:
• "Henpecked husband" refers to a man who is constantly dominated or controlled by his wife.

• The best match is "oppressed husband," as it implies a husband who is controlled or subdued.

Other options:

• (1) Controlling husband → Incorrect, as "henpecked" means the opposite.

• (2) Bossy husbands → Incorrect, as the wife is usually the bossy one in this context.

• (4) Dominating husbands → Incorrect, as a "henpecked husband" is submissive, not dominant.

questions.q_hi:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom:

This year's budget is unlikely to pass as law since the president's proposed budgets typically face a jaundiced eye, but this one has gotten even more skepticism.
questions.solution_en:
· The idiom "a jaundiced eye" means looking at something with suspicion, bias, or resentment.

· Jealousy (Option 1) is a strong emotion but does not fit well here.

· Confidence (Option 2) is the opposite of skepticism.

· Goodwill (Option 4) means positive feelings, which contradicts skepticism.

Thus, the correct answer is Resentment.

questions.q_en:
Complete the dialogue for Person B using the correct idiom.

Person A: I am so nervous. I don't think I should make the speech tomorrow.

Person B: No. You are just getting ______. You have prepared for this.
questions.q_hi:
Complete the dialogue for Person B using the correct idiom.

Person A: I am so nervous. I don't think I should make the speech tomorrow.

Person B: No. You are just getting ______. You have prepared for this.
questions.solution_en: The context suggests Person A is nervous and considering backing out of the speech. The idiom "getting cold feet" means becoming nervous or hesitant about a planned action, fitting perfectly. Person B reassures A that their nervousness is just hesitation and they are prepared. "Hot feet" is not a standard idiom, "cold hand" relates to poor circulation or fear in a different context, and "cold foot" is incorrect. Thus, "cold feet" is the correct choice.
